A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CoMM research. All 22 pages of each version, including equations, tables, figures, and appendices, support comparison; retained content can be matched across reformatting and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original dataset-quality assessments, downstream few-shot experiments, and quantitative and qualitative generation results in Tables 1–3 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds preference-training experiments, filtering and scaling studies, an independent model evaluation, and human ratings.

M1.justification: v2 adds preference-dataset construction using four forms of text, image, and step shuffling, followed by DPO training of SEED-Llama after supervised fine-tuning. This introduces a substantive additional training procedure; the original filtering pipeline and supervised model configurations remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds preferred/dispreferred sequence pairs actually used for preference training, extending training beyond the supervised generation setup. The five data sources, seven downstream benchmarks, and four generation tasks remain unchanged. The topic chart and storytelling example concern already represented domains.

E2.justification: Tables 4 and 6 introduce comparisons between DPO-trained SEED-Llama 8B/14B variants and their supervised-only counterparts. The MMC4/OBELICS comparisons and original MiniGPT-5, SEED-Llama, and Emu2 comparisons are retained. Claude-3.5-Sonnet is an added evaluator, not a competing generation baseline.

E3.justification: v2 adds filtering-threshold sweeps and dataset-fraction experiments evaluated through 16-shot captioning, Claude-3.5-Sonnet assessments of 5,000 documents per dataset, and Task 4 ratings from 32 people. These substantially extend the evaluation design. Original benchmark splits, metrics, shot settings, and supervised training settings are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix B tests sensitivity to ITA and image-sequence filtering thresholds, training-data scale, filtering-model bias through an independent evaluator, and GPT-4o evaluation through human ratings. Figure 10 also adds a storytelling case comparison. These analyses were absent from v1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. The new human participant count describes sample size; the human study adds no inter-rater agreement or uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1–3 retain their numerical results. v2 adds substantial results in Tables 4 and 6–11. For example, newly evaluated DPO training gives SEED-Llama 14B Task 1 step METEOR 4.62 versus supervised-only 3.16, but Task 2 FID worsens to 72.60 versus 66.23. These are additional training-condition comparisons, not revisions to the original scores.

T1.justification: The image-sequence metric and four task formulations in Equations 1–5 retain the same mathematical content. DPO is introduced operationally and by citation, without a new formal derivation, theorem, assumption, or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract is unchanged, and the central claims about coherent interleaved data, multimodal capabilities, and four benchmark tasks remain. The introduction and third contribution additionally claim that CoMM supports both supervised fine-tuning and preference training.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning evaluator bias, human validation, acquisition costs limiting dataset scale, and DPO's stronger utility for text than image generation. Its human-agreement interpretation is overstated: Table 11 reverses Emu2's Task 4 trend and image-quality rankings relative to GPT-4o's Table 3.

D1.justification: v2 discloses DPO's learning rate of 5×10−7, batch size 16, and beta 0.05, and identifies an ITA cutoff of 4 and preferred ImgS threshold of 1.0. These filtering disclosures do not establish changes to earlier experiments. Original training details, evaluation prompts, access information, and license terms are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to preference-learning and RLHF surveys and to DPO, supporting its new positioning around preference-based post-training. The existing related-work discussion and cited research are otherwise retained apart from bibliographic formatting and numbering.

P1.justification: Most existing prose remains intact. v2 shortens and rewrites the conclusion, adds preference-training passages, and introduces an appendix roadmap and dedicated additional-experiments section. Retained appendix sections are renumbered rather than removed.

P2.justification: v2 substantially reformats the document from single-column to two-column presentation, reflowing captions, tables, and prompt boxes. It adds preference-training and validation tables, a topic-distribution chart, and a storytelling figure. Original appendix Figures 5–8 are retained as Figures 6–9.

improvement.justification: The filtering and scaling experiments and independent Claude evaluation strengthen support for the dataset-quality claims beyond v1. Reporting DPO's text-generation benefits alongside image-generation shortcomings also improves informativeness. These gains are tempered by weak human-validation interpretation: Emu2 ranks first under GPT-4o but last under human ratings for trend and image quality, contrary to the broad agreement claim. Missing agreement and uncertainty estimates further limit that validation.
